question: How would you add multi-tenancy to this workflow engine, and how do Temporal namespaces solve isolation?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha jawab: is project mein multi-tenancy implement nahi hai -- `SECURITY.md` clearly bolta hai "not supported (single namespace); Temporal uses namespaces for isolation". Saare workflows ek hi `workflows` table mein hain, `workflow_id` globally unique hai, aur koi bhi caller kisi bhi workflow ko signal ya cancel kar sakta hai.

Production mein main isko teen layers mein add karunga. Pehla, data model: `workflows` ka primary key `(namespace, workflow_id)` banana, aur `history_events`, `activity_tasks`, `timers` sab mein namespace column. Isse do tenants ka `order-123` collide nahi karega, aur idempotent start bhi per-namespace ho jayega. Doosra, authorization: API pe service auth (mTLS ya JWT) aur har request ka namespace caller ki identity se derive karna, body se nahi. Teesra, resource isolation: per-namespace task queues aur rate limits, taaki ek noisy tenant ke 10,000 workflows doosre tenant ka `needs_task` backlog block na karein -- abhi `claim_workflow_task` `ORDER BY workflow_id` karta hai, toh koi fairness nahi hai.

Temporal mein namespace ek first-class unit hai: har namespace ki apni retention period, apni archival config, apne search attributes, aur authorizer plugin namespace-level permissions check karta hai. Workers ek specific namespace + task queue se hi poll karte hain. Bahut strong isolation chahiye (regulated tenants) toh alag cluster ya alag database bhi diya jata hai -- yeh "silo" model hai, namespace "pool" model hai.

Interview mein main honestly bolunga: demo internal single-tenant service hai; multi-tenant banane ka sabse sasta pehla step namespace column + auth-derived namespace hai.
why_needed: SaaS ya platform team ka shared workflow engine kai teams/customers serve karta hai; bina isolation ek team doosri ka workflow cancel kar sakti hai ya uske data padh sakti hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek building mein kai offices: lift aur bijli shared (pool), par har office ka apna taala aur apna mail box (namespace). Bank vault chahiye toh alag building (silo).
how_it_works: Namespace = har table ke key ka prefix + auth boundary + quota boundary. Request aate hi identity -> namespace resolve, phir har query `WHERE namespace = :ns` ke saath. Per-namespace retention aur task queues noisy-neighbour rokte hain.
in_this_project: `SECURITY.md` mein multi-tenancy "not supported (single namespace)" listed hai. `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` mein `workflows.workflow_id text PRIMARY KEY` hai -- globally unique, koi tenant column nahi. `api.py::signal` aur `api.py::cancel` kisi auth ke bina sirf workflow_id lete hain. `config.py` ka `admin_token` sirf operator route `retry-task` protect karta hai -- tenant identity nahi deta.
advantages: Tenants ke business ids collide nahi karte
Per-tenant retention, quotas aur permissions possible
disadvantages: Har query aur index mein extra column
Cross-tenant admin tooling complex
Migration existing data ke liye painful
common_mistakes: Namespace request body se lena (caller koi bhi namespace bhej dega)
Sirf API pe check karna, workers ko kisi bhi namespace ka task claim karne dena
Per-tenant fairness bhool jana
follow_up_questions: Pool vs silo isolation kab choose karoge?
Per-namespace fairness claim query mein kaise laoge?
Namespace-level encryption keys kaise manage karoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Shared tables (pool) saste aur simple hain par blast radius bada; alag DB/cluster (silo) strong isolation deta hai par operational cost multiply hota hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar auth se namespace derive nahi hua toh cross-tenant signal/cancel possible. Ek tenant ka backlog shared pollers ko starve kar sakta hai kyunki claim ORDER BY workflow_id hai.
advanced.alternatives: Row-level security (Postgres RLS) namespace pe; per-tenant schema; per-tenant cluster (Temporal Cloud jaisa).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x tenants: namespace column + quotas kaafi. 100x: namespaces ko history shards/DBs pe distribute karna, big tenants ko dedicated shards.
advanced.production_improvements: mTLS + identity-to-namespace mapping, per-namespace rate limits, per-namespace retention + archival, audit log of signal/cancel calls.

question: How does this project protect against XSS in the dashboard and SQL injection in the store?
answer_hinglish:
Do classic web risks hain aur dono yahan handle hain. XSS ke liye `flowengine/dashboard.html` mein ek `esc()` helper hai jo `& < > "` ko HTML entities mein convert karta hai, aur workflow_id, type, error, worker_id jaisi saari user-controlled values `innerHTML` mein jaane se pehle `esc()` se guzarti hain. History panel `textContent` use karta hai, jo HTML parse hi nahi karta -- woh by design safe hai. Yeh important hai kyunki workflow_id aur signal payload client deta hai; koi `<script>` wala workflow_id bana de toh dashboard dekhne wale operator ke browser mein code chal sakta tha.

SQL injection ke liye `store.py` aur `api.py` dono SQLAlchemy `text()` ke saath bound parameters (`:w`, `:s`, `:q`) use karte hain. JSON values `CAST(:a AS jsonb)` se jaati hain, string concatenation se nahi. `api.py::list_workflows` mein query string dynamic banti hai, par sirf fixed SQL fragment (`WHERE status = :s`) append hota hai; status value phir bhi parameter hai.

Honest observation: `tests/conftest.py::effects` test helper `WHERE kind = '{kind}'` f-string se banata hai. Yeh sirf tests mein hai aur input hardcoded hai, isliye real risk nahi, par code review mein main isko bhi parameterise karwata -- bad pattern copy hote hain. `SECURITY.md` "Dashboard XSS: all values escaped" aur "SQL injection: parameterised queries throughout" claim karta hai, jo production code ke liye sahi hai.
why_needed: Dashboard operators use karte hain jinke paas high privilege hota hai; unke browser mein XSS matlab engine ka control. SQL injection matlab poori history/DB compromise.
real_world_analogy: Parameterised query aise hai jaise form mein 'naam' wala box -- aap usmein kuch bhi likho, woh naam hi maana jayega, command nahi. Escaping aise hai jaise poster pe kisi ki likhi baat ko quote marks mein chhapna.
how_it_works: Bound parameters DB driver alag se bhejta hai, SQL parser unhe kabhi code nahi samajhta. `esc()` special characters ko entities mein badalta hai taaki browser unhe text dikhaye, tags nahi.
in_this_project: `flowengine/dashboard.html` ka `esc` function aur `showHist` mein `textContent`. `flowengine/store.py` mein har query `text(...)` + dict params. `flowengine/api.py::list_workflows` ka status filter parameterised. Gap: `tests/conftest.py::effects` mein f-string SQL.

question: What abuse vectors exist through workflow inputs and signal payloads (size, volume, unbounded endpoints), and how would you harden them?
answer_hinglish:
Inputs aur signals "data" hain, code nahi, isliye code execution ka risk nahi -- par resource abuse ka risk zaroor hai. Teen vectors main dekhta hoon.

Pehla, payload size: `StartIn.input` aur `SignalIn.payload` `Any` type hain, koi size limit nahi. Har signal `SignalReceived` event ban ke `history_events` mein permanently jaata hai, aur har workflow task poori history padh ke replay karta hai. Toh koi 5MB ke 1000 signals bhej de toh DB bloat bhi hoga aur har replay slow -- TESTING.md dikhata hai 2,001 events pe replay 102-132 ms le leta hai, payload bhaari ho toh aur zyada.

Doosra, volume: signal endpoint pe koi rate limit nahi. Har signal `needs_task = true` set karta hai, toh signal flood = workflow-task flood = CPU-bound replay storm. Temporal isi wajah se history size/count limits rakhta hai (warning thresholds aur hard limit pe workflow terminate).

Teesra, unbounded reads: `/workflows/{id}/history` mein pagination nahi hai, poori history ek response mein aati hai. `list_workflows` mein `limit` le=1000 tak capped hai, jo achha hai.

Hardening: pydantic mein payload size validate karna (ya request body limit at proxy), per-workflow signal count/size limit `store.signal` mein (lock ke andar last_event_id check karke reject), API pe rate limiting (Project 1 ka limiter reuse), history endpoint pe `after_event_id` + `limit` pagination, aur bade blobs ko object storage mein rakh ke history mein sirf reference.
why_needed: Workflow engine ki history permanent aur replay-critical hai; usmein kachra bhar gaya toh woh workflow hamesha ke liye slow ho jata hai.
real_world_analogy: Register mein har visitor ki entry likhni hai. Koi har minute 100 visitors bheje, ya har entry 10 page ki ho, toh register bhar jayega aur har audit mein poora register padhna padega.
how_it_works: History append-only aur replay full hai, toh har byte jo history mein jaata hai woh har future workflow task mein dobara padha jayega. Isliye input pe limit lagana storage aur CPU dono bachata hai.
in_this_project: `flowengine/api.py::StartIn` mein `input: Any` aur `SignalIn` mein `payload: Any` -- size validation nahi. `store.signal` har signal ko history mein append karta hai aur `needs_task = true`. `api.py::history` unpaginated hai. `list_workflows` ka `limit` `Query(100, ge=1, le=1000)` bounded hai. Yeh sab limits is project mein implement nahi hain.

async def signal(sm, workflow_id, name, payload):
    if len(_j(payload)) > MAX_PAYLOAD:

    async with sm() as s, s.begin():

disadvantages: Legit bade payloads ko alag storage chahiye

Bade documents history mein embed karna
History endpoint unpaginated chhodna

Payload ko object storage mein offload kaise karoge?

advanced.failure_scenarios: Signal flood -> needs_task har baar true -> CPU-bound replays queue up; badi history -> har replay mehenga; unpaginated history -> API memory spike.
advanced.alternatives: Claim-check (blob store + reference), per-workflow signal quota, gateway rate limits, Temporal ki tarah blob size limit + history count limit.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x pe history size directly replay CPU aur DB storage multiply karta hai; limits ke bina ek bad client poore cluster ko slow kar sakta hai.

question: Why replay deterministic code against history instead of simply storing the workflow's state after each step?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh is project ka central design decision hai. Alternative simple lagta hai: har step ke baad state (variables, current step) DB mein save karo, crash pe wahin se resume. Problem yeh hai ki Python coroutine ka state -- local variables, call stack, kahan await pe ruka hai -- serialize nahi hota. Toh state store karne ke liye aapko workflow ko explicit state machine mein likhna padta (Step Functions JSON, ya `if step == 3` wala code). Code readable nahi rehta, try/except compensation natural nahi rehta.

Replay approach mein hum sirf facts store karte hain (`ActivityCompleted seq 2 result X`). State hamesha derive hoti hai: code ko shuru se chalao aur results feed karo. Fayde: workflow plain async Python hai (`order_processing` mein normal try/except saga), koi bhi worker kisi bhi workflow ko continue kar sakta hai, poora audit trail free mein, aur races deterministic (`test_race_signal_first_wins`).

Cost do hain. Ek, determinism rules -- `ctx.now()`, `ctx.random()`, no I/O; galti hui toh NonDeterminismError. Do, CPU: har workflow task full replay karta hai, aur TESTING.md mein measured hai 21 events ~0.5 ms, 201 ~3.4 ms, 2,001 ~102 ms -- super-linear. `TRADEOFFS.md` #1 aur #2 yahi likhte hain.

Main bolunga: developer ergonomics aur correctness ke liye replay jeeta; CPU cost ko production engines sticky cache aur continue-as-new se manage karte hain. Ek middle ground bhi hai -- snapshotting -- par Python coroutines ke saath woh possible nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer yeh dekhna chahta hai ki aap event sourcing ka 'kyun' samajhte ho, sirf 'kya' nahi.
real_world_analogy: Chess game ka board photo (state) vs moves ki list (history). Moves ki list se board kabhi bhi dobara bana sakte ho, kisi bhi table pe, aur pata bhi hai kaise yahan pahunche.
how_it_works: Store: append-only events. Execute: `replay()` coroutine start karta hai, events order mein feed karta hai, code wahin pahunch jaata hai jahan pichhli baar tha, phir naye commands nikalte hain. Coroutine discard ho jaata hai (`task.cancel()` in finally).
in_this_project: `flowengine/runtime.py::replay` docstring yahi loop describe karta hai; `replay` ke `finally` mein coroutine cancel hota hai -- "next task replays from scratch". `TRADEOFFS.md` points 1-2, `bench/bench.py::replay_cost` cost measure karta hai. `test_worker_crash_another_worker_resumes_from_history` prove karta hai ki memory mein kuch nahi chahiye.

# real, flowengine/runtime.py (end of replay)
finally:
    if not task.done():
        task.cancel()     # the coroutine is discarded; next task replays from scratch
advantages: Workflow plain code hai, state machine nahi
disadvantages: Determinism discipline zaroori
Replay CPU history ke saath badhta hai
Code changes versioning maangte hain
common_mistakes: Replay ko 'har baar activities dobara chalana' samajhna -- activities replay nahi hoti, sirf results feed hote hain
Determinism cost ko ignore karna
State aur history dono store karke unhe out-of-sync kar dena
follow_up_questions: Sticky cache replay ko kaise bachata hai?
Snapshot kyun nahi le sakte Python coroutine ka?
Continue-as-new kab use karoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Replay: ergonomic code + stateless workers vs CPU cost + determinism rules. Stored state: cheap resume vs explicit state machines aur serialization problems.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Replay mein bad deploy = NonDeterminismError (workflow blocked). Stored state mein bad deploy = purana state naye code se mismatch, silent corruption possible.
advanced.alternatives: AWS Step Functions (state machine JSON), Azure Durable Functions (replay, jaisa yeh), Camunda (BPMN + DB state), Airflow (DAG task state).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: sticky cache se replay sirf cache miss pe. 100x: history sharding + continue-as-new, kyunki ek workflow ki history bhi bound karni padti hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Sticky worker cache, continue-as-new, history length alerts, replay tests in CI against recorded production histories.

question: What are the trade-offs of using one Postgres database for history, task queues, timers and worker registry?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein Postgres hi sab kuch hai: `history_events` (event store), `workflows.needs_task` (workflow-task queue), `activity_tasks` (activity queue with `visible_at` backoff), `timers` (durable timers), aur `workers` (registry). `TRADEOFFS.md` #3 isko explicitly trade-off bolta hai.

Sabse bada fayda: transactions. `complete_workflow_task` ek hi transaction mein history events append karta hai, activity tasks insert karta hai, timers insert karta hai aur `needs_task` clear karta hai. Agar queue alag system (Redis/Kafka) hota toh yeh dual-write ban jaata -- event likha par task enqueue nahi hua, ya ulta -- aur outbox pattern chahiye hota. Yahan woh problem exist hi nahi karti. Doosra fayda: inspect karna easy -- ek SQL query se workflow ka poora state dikh jaata hai, dashboard bhi wahi karta hai.

Cost: Postgres bottleneck banta hai. TESTING.md ke hisaab se ek 4-activity workflow ~97 SQL statements leta hai, aur processes badhane pe throughput 4.9 -> 7.6 -> 8.3 workflows/s pe flatten hota dikh raha hai (shared Postgres, Docker Desktop on Windows). Polling se idle queries bhi aati hain. Aur queue tables pe heavy UPDATE churn se dead tuples/vacuum pressure hota hai (yeh general Postgres behaviour hai, measured nahi).

Production answer: chhote/medium scale pe yeh bilkul theek hai (bahut log pg-boss, river jaise Postgres queues use karte hain). Bade scale pe Temporal ki tarah history ko shards mein baanto aur matching (task queues) ko alag in-memory service banao.
why_needed: Interviewer check karta hai ki aap 'ek DB' ko lazy choice nahi, conscious consistency choice ki tarah defend kar sakte ho.
real_world_analogy: Chhoti dukaan mein ek hi register mein stock, orders aur udhaar -- sab consistent, ek jagah. Dukaan mall ban jaaye toh alag departments aur alag registers chahiye.
how_it_works: Har state change ek Postgres transaction hai jo workflow row lock leta hai; queues `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` se claim hoti hain; backoff `visible_at` column se; timers `fire_at` index se poll hote hain.
in_this_project: `flowengine/store.py::complete_workflow_task` ek transaction mein events + `activity_tasks` + `timers` likhta hai. `TRADEOFFS.md` #3 aur TESTING.md ka "97 SQL statements per workflow". `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` mein saari tables.
advantages: Atomic multi-table updates, koi dual-write nahi
disadvantages: Single DB throughput ceiling
Polling overhead
Queue churn se vacuum pressure
common_mistakes: Queue ko Redis mein daal ke transactional guarantee kho dena bina outbox ke
97 statements ko ignore karke 'Postgres slow hai' bolna -- pehle statements kam karo
Sabhi workers ka pool size DB max_connections se zyada

Outbox pattern kab chahiye hota?

question: Why does the workflow task use an optimistic commit (check last_event_id) instead of holding a row lock during replay?
answer_hinglish:
Do options the. Pessimistic: workflow row `FOR UPDATE` lock lo, replay karo, commit karo -- sab ek transaction mein. Optimistic (jo yahan hai): claim karte waqt lease lo aur history `last_event_id = N` tak padho, transaction band karo, replay transaction ke bahar karo, phir commit ke waqt row lock lo aur check karo ki `last_event_id` abhi bhi N hai. Agar nahi -- matlab beech mein signal, activity completion ya timer aa gaya -- toh result discard, `needs_task` true rehta hai, aur task naye events ke saath dobara chalega.

Optimistic kyun? Replay pure CPU hai aur history badi ho toh 100 ms+ le sakta hai (TESTING.md: 2,001 events pe 102-132 ms). Agar us poore time row lock pakda rahe toh `store.signal`, `complete_activity`, `fire_due_timers` -- sab jo workflow row lock karte hain -- block ho jaate. Matlab activity worker ka completion commit bhi ruk jaata. Aur long transactions Postgres mein connection pin karti hain aur vacuum ko rokti hain.

Cost: occasional wasted replay. Jab signal race karta hai toh ek replay bekaar jaata hai. `TRADEOFFS.md` #5 yahi likhta hai: "No long locks during replay; occasionally wasted replays when signals race". Kyunki replay deterministic hai, dobara chalana hamesha safe hai -- koi side effect nahi.

Yeh `test_stale_workflow_task_is_discarded_when_history_moves` prove karta hai: claim, replay, beech mein signal, phir `complete_workflow_task` False return karta hai aur koi activity task create nahi hota.
why_needed: Locking strategy throughput aur latency pe seedha asar daalti hai; interviewer optimistic concurrency control ka practical use dekhna chahta hai.
real_world_analogy: Google Doc offline edit: aap version 5 pe kaam karte ho; save karte waqt agar server pe version 6 aa chuka hai toh aapka save reject, refresh karke dobara. Poore editing time document lock nahi kiya.
how_it_works: `claim_workflow_task` lease + snapshot (N). `replay` bahar. `complete_workflow_task` -> `_lock` -> compare `current["last_event_id"] != wf["last_event_id"]` -> mismatch pe sirf apni lease release (`AND locked_by = :k`) aur False.
in_this_project: `flowengine/store.py::complete_workflow_task` ki pehli lines; `store.py` module docstring "Workflow task protocol (optimistic)". `Worker.run_workflow_task_once` mein `stats["stale"] += 1` jab commit reject ho. Test: `tests/test_engine.py::test_stale_workflow_task_is_discarded_when_history_moves`.

# real, flowengine/store.py complete_workflow_task
current = await _lock(s, wid)
if current["last_event_id"] != wf["last_event_id"] or current["status"] != "running":
    # Only release the lease if it is still ours (another worker may have claimed it after expiry)
    await s.execute(text("UPDATE workflows SET locked_by = NULL, lease_until = NULL WHERE workflow_id = :w "
                         "AND locked_by = :k"), {"w": wid, "k": wf["locked_by"]})
    return False
advantages: Row lock milliseconds ke liye, replay ke duration ke liye nahi
Activity completions aur signals block nahi hote
Deterministic replay ki wajah se retry safe
disadvantages: Signal-heavy workflows mein wasted replays
Extra state (last_event_id) maintain karna
common_mistakes: Version check ke bina commit -- stale commands append ho jaate
Replay ke andar DB transaction open rakhna
Mismatch pe needs_task clear kar dena (event lost)

question: Why does a NonDeterminismError leave the workflow running and blocked instead of failing it?
answer_hinglish:
Non-determinism ka matlab hai ki naya code purani history se match nahi karta -- almost hamesha yeh code bug ya bad deploy hai, workflow ki business failure nahi. Agar hum workflow ko `failed` kar dete toh woh terminal hai: customer ka order beech mein mar gaya, compensation bhi nahi chalegi, aur rollback karne se bhi wapas nahi aayega.

Isliye `complete_workflow_task` mein jab `outcome is None` (replay hi fail hua) hota hai, hum sirf `error` column mein message likhte hain, `needs_task = false` aur lease clear karte hain -- status `running` rehta hai aur history mein kuch append nahi hota. Comment explicitly bolta hai: "it stays running and blocked so it can resume once correct code is deployed (Temporal does the same)". Temporal mein bhi default behaviour yahi hai: workflow task fail hota hai aur retry hota rehta hai jab tak code fix na ho.

`test_nondeterministic_deploy_is_detected_and_workflow_survives` poori kahani prove karta hai: v1 se ek step chala, v2 deploy hua jismein ek naya activity step pehle insert hai, worker ne `nondeterminism` stat badhaya, status `running` aur error mein `NonDeterminismError`. Phir v1 wapas (rollback), `store.retry_workflow_task(...)` (needs_task = true), aur workflow `done` result ke saath complete.

Trade-off: blocked workflows chupchap pade reh sakte hain, isliye `error` field pe alerting zaroori hai (`DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 3). Blocked hone ke baad `needs_task` false hai; fix deploy karne ke baad automatic re-trigger nahi hai. Pehle iske liye manual SQL UPDATE hi rasta tha -- review mein yeh gap mila aur ab operator endpoint `POST /workflows/{id}/retry-task` (X-Admin-Token) hai, test `test_retry_task_requeues_only_running_workflows`.
why_needed: Bad deploys inevitable hain; system ka behaviour aisa hona chahiye ki rollback se recovery ho, data loss se nahi.
real_world_analogy: Train ka signal kharab ho gaya toh train ko scrap nahi karte; platform pe rok dete ho, signal theek karo, train aage chal padti hai.
how_it_works: Worker `NonDeterminismError` pakadta hai -> `complete_workflow_task(sm, wf, None, error)` -> error set, needs_task false, status untouched. Fixed code + needs_task true -> agla replay normal.
in_this_project: `flowengine/worker.py::run_workflow_task_once` ka `except NonDeterminismError` branch; `flowengine/store.py::complete_workflow_task` ka `if outcome is None` block. Test: `tests/test_engine.py::test_nondeterministic_deploy_is_detected_and_workflow_survives`. `TRADEOFFS.md` #6.
code_example:
# real, flowengine/store.py
if outcome is None:
    # Replay itself failed (e.g. non-determinism after a bad deploy): the workflow is NOT failed -- it stays
    # running and blocked so it can resume once correct code is deployed (Temporal does the same).
    await s.execute(text("UPDATE workflows SET error = :e, needs_task = false, locked_by = NULL, lease_until = NULL "
                         "WHERE workflow_id = :w"), {"e": error, "w": wid})
    return True

question: Why does the determinism check compare only command and activity types, not arguments? What does that miss?
answer_hinglish:
`replay()` mein jab history ka `ActivityScheduled` event aata hai toh code ka command same `seq` pe dhoondha jaata hai aur sirf `activity_type` compare hota hai. `TimerStarted` ke liye sirf `kind == "start_timer"` check hota hai, duration nahi. Arguments (amount, email, template) compare nahi hote.

Kyun? Teen reasons. Ek, cheap -- string compare, koi serialization nahi. Do, Temporal bhi yahi karta hai: command type aur activity type match hona chahiye, input nahi, kyunki arguments legitimately change ho sakte hain (jaise ek bug fix jo email template ka naam theek kare) aur us change se running workflows ko block karna overkill hai. Teen, arguments mein aksar workflow ke derived values hote hain; compare karne ke liye unhe canonical serialize karna padta.

Kya miss hota hai: same type ka step insert karna. `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` bug 5 aur test comment yahi bolta hai -- agar v2 mein ek naya `notify` step pehle insert ho jaaye toh replay pe seq 1 ka type `notify` hi hai, check pass, aur purane result naye step ko mil jaate hain. Workflow galat data ke saath chalta rahega. Isliye test `archive_document` (different type) insert karta hai. Argument changes bhi undetected: amount 100 se 200 ho gaya toh history mein charged 100 hai par code sochta hai 200.

`TRADEOFFS.md` #7 isko "Cheap and matches Temporal; argument changes go undetected" bolta hai. Mitigation: versioning (`patched()`), aur CI mein replay tests.
why_needed: Determinism check ki limitations pata na hon toh developer false confidence mein deploy kar deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Attendance mein sirf roll number check kiya, naam nahi. Roll 5 pe koi aur baith gaya toh pata nahi chalega.
how_it_works: Seq numbers command order se assign hote hain (`_next`). History event ka seq aur type -> code ka command at same seq -> type equal? Sirf yahi.
in_this_project: `flowengine/runtime.py::replay` ka `if et in ("ActivityScheduled", "TimerStarted")` block. `tests/test_engine.py::test_nondeterministic_deploy_is_detected_and_workflow_survives` ka comment same-type insert ke baare mein. `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` bug 5, `TRADEOFFS.md` #7, README known limitations.

question: Why are activities at-least-once with an idempotency key instead of using distributed transactions with external systems?
answer_hinglish:
Activity ka kaam external world mein side effect karna hai -- payment provider, email service. Inke saath distributed transaction (2PC) practically possible nahi: Stripe ya SMTP server aapke Postgres ke saath XA transaction mein participate nahi karte. Toh exactly-once delivery ki guarantee nahi di ja sakti.

Is project ka model: activity at-least-once chalti hai. Worker crash ho, lease expire ho, ya result commit hone se pehle network gire -- activity dobara chalegi. Isliye har activity ko `ActivityContext.idempotency_key = "<workflow_id>:<seq>"` milta hai jo retries aur redeliveries mein same rehta hai. Activity author is key ko downstream ko deta hai (payment provider ka Idempotency-Key header) ya apne DB mein unique key ki tarah use karta hai. Example activities `effect()` helper se `activity_effects` mein `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` karti hain -- effect ek hi baar.

Tests isko prove karte hain: `test_retries_with_backoff_then_success_effect_once` mein charge 3 attempts leta hai par `{"charge": 1}`; heartbeat test mein worker crash ke baad attempt 2 par `{"long_task": 1}`.

Trade-off (`TRADEOFFS.md` #9): engine simple aur available rehta hai, koi coordinator nahi; par responsibility activity author pe hai -- agar woh key ignore kare toh duplicates honge. Engine ise enforce nahi kar sakta. Ek subtle point: key `workflow_id:seq` hai, run_id nahi -- toh agar future mein same workflow_id reuse hua (naya run) toh keys collide karengi; abhi `start_workflow` workflow_id reuse allow nahi karta, isliye safe hai.
why_needed: Exactly-once ka myth interviews mein common trap hai; sahi jawab hai at-least-once + idempotent effects.
real_world_analogy: Courier ka tracking number: courier do baar bhi aaye toh receiver dekhta hai 'yeh parcel number pehle hi mila', dobara sign nahi karta.
how_it_works: Key deterministic hai (workflow_id + command seq), toh har attempt ko same key milti hai. Downstream unique constraint ya provider dedupe pehli successful effect ke baad baaki ko no-op kar deta hai.
in_this_project: `flowengine/worker.py::_execute` key banata hai `f"{task['workflow_id']}:{task['seq']}"`. `flowengine/activities.py::ActivityContext` mein `idempotency_key`. `flowengine/examples/activities.py::effect` ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Tests: `test_retries_with_backoff_then_success_effect_once`, `test_activity_heartbeat_timeout_detects_dead_worker`.

async def effect(ctx: ActivityContext, kind: str, payload: dict) -> bool:
    async with ctx.sm() as s, s.begin():
        row = await s.scalar(text("INSERT INTO activity_effects (idempotency_key, kind, payload) VALUES (:k, :t, CAST(:p AS jsonb)) "
                                  "ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING idempotency_key"),
                             {"k": ctx.idempotency_key, "t": kind, "p": json.dumps(payload)})
    return row is not None

question: Why build a workflow engine instead of using Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Airflow or Camunda? When would you pick each?
answer_hinglish:
Honest jawab: production mein main khud ka engine nahi banata -- Temporal (ya managed Temporal Cloud) use karta. Yeh project learning ke liye hai: durable execution ke internals (event history, replay, determinism, leases, fencing) ko itna samajhna ki Temporal ke behaviour ko predict aur debug kar sakoon. README khud ise "Temporal-style" bolta hai aur limitations list karta hai: no sticky cache, no versioning API, no child workflows, single Postgres.

Kaunsa kab: Temporal -- jab business process code mein likhna ho, long-running (din/mahine), signals, compensations, high reliability; cost hai cluster operate karna (ya Cloud ka bill) aur determinism discipline. AWS Step Functions -- AWS-native, serverless, state machine JSON/ASL mein; chhote orchestration ke liye great, par complex logic JSON mein awkward aur per-transition pricing. Airflow -- data pipelines aur batch DAGs, schedule-driven; per-request business workflows (har order ek workflow) ke liye nahi bana, latency seconds-minutes. Camunda/Zeebe -- BPMN, jahan business analysts diagram se process define karte hain aur human tasks heavy hain.

Kab khud ka banaoge? Jab requirements bahut chhoti hon (2-3 step saga) aur already Postgres hai -- tab ek simple outbox + state table kaafi hai, poora engine nahi. Ya jab extreme constraints hon (embedded, air-gapped). Isliye interview mein main bolunga: 'Maine yeh banaya taaki Temporal ko black box nahi, glass box ki tarah samjhoon.'
why_needed: Senior interviews mein build-vs-buy judgement dekha jaata hai; 'maine banaya' ke saath 'production mein kya use karunga' bolna maturity dikhata hai.
real_world_analogy: Car ka engine khol ke dobara jodna mechanic banne ke liye zaroori hai; par office jaane ke liye aap company ki banayi car hi chalate ho.
how_it_works: Decision factors: process ki lambai, kaun define karta hai (dev vs analyst), cloud lock-in, ops capacity, latency, aur failure semantics.
in_this_project: `README.md` "Known limitations" aur title "Temporal-style". `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` workflow vs job queue table. `TRADEOFFS.md` poore design choices. Engine ~250 lines `runtime.py` + ~290 lines `store.py` -- learning-sized.

Khud ka engine maintain karna mehenga
Ecosystem/tooling nahi
common_mistakes: Har problem ke liye Airflow use karna (per-entity workflows ke liye galat)
2-step process ke liye Temporal cluster lagana
Khud ka engine production mein daal dena bina versioning/sharding ke

question: How do you safely deploy a change to workflow code when workflows are already running?
answer_hinglish:
Running workflows ki history purane code ne likhi hai, aur replay naye code se hoga. Agar naya code alag commands produce kare (step insert/remove/reorder) toh NonDeterminismError aur workflow blocked. Toh deploy process mein teen cheezein chahiye.

Pehla, detect before deploy: `POST /workflows/{id}/replay-check` current code ko recorded history pe replay karta hai aur `{deterministic: bool}` deta hai. `DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 1 kehta hai isse CI mein chalao. Better: production se kuch real histories export karke test suite mein replay karo (Temporal ka "replayer" bhi yahi karta hai).

Doosra, versioning: purane runs purana path lein, naye runs naya. Temporal mein `workflow.patched("add-fraud-check")` -- naye run mein marker event record hota hai aur true return karta hai; purani history mein marker nahi toh false, aur code purana path chalta hai. Is project mein yeh implement nahi hai -- README "No workflow versioning API (patched())" bolta hai. Workaround: naya workflow type register karo (`order_processing_v2`) aur naye starts usse karo, purane drain hone do.

Teesra, safe changes pehchano: activity ke andar ka code change hamesha safe hai (activities replay nahi hoti). Workflow ke end mein naya step add karna jo abhi tak koi run nahi pahuncha woh bhi effectively safe. Args change type-level check pass karega par semantically galat ho sakta hai.

Agar galti ho bhi jaaye: workflow fail nahi hota, blocked rehta hai; rollback karo aur `needs_task` reset karo -- `test_nondeterministic_deploy_is_detected_and_workflow_survives` yahi dikhata hai.
why_needed: Long-running workflows (din/mahine) ka matlab hai har deploy pe running workflows hongi; yeh durable execution ka sabse bada operational risk hai.
real_world_analogy: Chalti train ka route change: jo trains already nikal chuki hain unhe purane route pe jaane do, naye route pe sirf nayi trains bhejo.
how_it_works: replay-check = dry-run replay without writes. Versioning = history mein marker se branch decide karna, deterministically. Type versioning = naya registry name.
in_this_project: `flowengine/api.py::replay_check` endpoint; `DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 1; README known limitations (no `patched()`). Worker mein `stats["nondeterminism"]` counter. Test: `tests/test_engine.py::test_nondeterministic_deploy_is_detected_and_workflow_survives`.

# CI step (illustrative): replay every running workflow against the new build
for wid in $(curl -s "$API/workflows?status=running&limit=1000" | jq -r '.workflows[].workflow_id'); do
  curl -s -X POST "$API/workflows/$wid/replay-check" | jq -e '.deterministic' >/dev/null || { echo "NON-DET: $wid"; exit 1; }
done

question: What would you monitor and alert on for this workflow engine in production?
answer_hinglish:
Workflow engine mein problems aksar "kuch nahi ho raha" ki shakal mein aati hain -- workflows chupchap ruk jaate hain. Isliye signals specifically choose karne padte hain. `DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 3 chaar cheezein list karta hai, aur main unhe aise explain karunga.

Ek, non-determinism: `workflows.error IS NOT NULL AND status = 'running'` -- yeh bad deploy ka sabse direct signal hai. Worker bhi `workflow_nondeterminism` error log aur `stats["nondeterminism"]` counter deta hai.

Do, workflow-task backlog: `/stats` endpoint `workflow_task_backlog` deta hai (running workflows with `needs_task`). Yeh badhta rahe toh workers kam hain ya replay slow hai.

Teen, activity attempts climbing: `activity_tasks.attempt` aur `last_error`. Bahut saare `ActivityTimeout` errors matlab workers crash ho rahe hain ya activities hang. Logs mein `activity_failed`, `activity_timeout` structured events hain.

Chaar, timer lag: `timers WHERE NOT fired AND fire_at < now() - interval '...'` -- agar timers time pe fire nahi ho rahe toh timer loop atka hai.

Plus: worker liveness via `/workers` (`seconds_since_heartbeat`), HTTP metrics `/metrics` (bpcommon ka Prometheus setup -- requests aur latency), aur DB metrics (connections, slow queries). Ek gap: engine-specific Prometheus metrics (backlog gauge, replay duration histogram) abhi nahi hain; worker stats sirf in-memory dict hai. Production mein main replay duration histogram zaroor add karunga kyunki replay cost history ke saath badhta hai.
why_needed: Durable engine ki failures silent hoti hain; bina alerts ke blocked workflows hafton pade reh sakte hain.
real_world_analogy: Hospital ward mein sirf 'patient chilla raha hai' pe dhyan dena kaafi nahi; pulse aur BP monitor chahiye jo chupchap girne pe bhi beep kare.
how_it_works: DB queries + /stats + structured JSON logs (bpcommon.logging) + HTTP Prometheus metrics. Alerts thresholds pe: error count > 0, backlog trend, timer lag > X seconds.
in_this_project: `flowengine/api.py::stats` (counts by status + backlog), `api.py::workers` (heartbeat age), `Worker.stats` dict, log events `workflow_nondeterminism`, `activity_failed`, `activity_timeout` in `worker.py`. `DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 3.

SELECT count(*) FROM timers WHERE NOT fired AND fire_at < now() - interval '30 seconds'; -- timer lag
SELECT activity_type, max(attempt) FROM activity_tasks WHERE status IN ('scheduled','started') GROUP BY 1;

Polling queries khud load dalti hain

question: Walk through the docker-compose deployment: migrations, API, workers, scaling and graceful shutdown.
answer_hinglish:
`docker-compose.yml` mein chaar services hain. `postgres` (17-alpine, named volume `pgdata`, `pg_isready` healthcheck). `migrate` -- same image, `alembic upgrade head` chalata hai aur tab chalta hai jab postgres healthy ho. `api` -- `migrate` ke `service_completed_successfully` hone ke baad start, sirf `127.0.0.1:58010` pe expose (internal service, public nahi). `worker` -- `python -m flowengine --activity-concurrency 16`, `replicas: 2`, aur `stop_grace_period: 15s`.

Ordering important hai: migration ek baar, alag one-shot container mein, taaki do API/worker replicas parallel mein migration na chalayein.

Scaling: workers stateless hain, toh `docker compose up -d --scale worker=4` kaafi hai -- koi rebalancing, koi sticky assignment nahi; SKIP LOCKED automatically kaam baant deta hai. TESTING.md dikhata hai processes add karne se throughput badhta hai (4.9 -> 7.6 -> 8.3 workflows/s), par shared Postgres pe flatten hota hai.

Graceful shutdown: Docker SIGTERM bhejta hai; `worker.main` mein signal handler `w.stop()` call karta hai. `Worker.run` ka finally pehle current workflow task complete karne deta hai (`shutdown_grace` 10s), phir in-flight activities ko 10s tak drain karta hai, phir deregister. `stop_grace_period: 15s` isliye hai ki Docker SIGKILL se pehle drain ka time mile. `DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 2: grace period >= longest activity jo aap drain karna chahte ho. Agar activity usse lambi hai toh SIGKILL aayega, lease expire hogi aur doosra worker retry karega -- correctness safe, bas ek wasted attempt.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki aap deploy order, migrations aur shutdown semantics ko distributed system ke angle se samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant shift change: naya staff aane se pehle kitchen setup (migration) ek baar; jaane wala cook haath ka order poora karke jaata hai (graceful), beech mein nahi bhaagta.
how_it_works: Compose depends_on conditions ordering enforce karti hain; SIGTERM -> stop event -> drain -> deregister; SIGKILL fallback pe lease-based recovery.
in_this_project: `docker-compose.yml` services aur `stop_grace_period: 15s`; `flowengine/worker.py::main` mein `loop.add_signal_handler(sig, w.stop)`; `Worker.run` finally block; `DEPLOYMENT.md`; `Dockerfile` non-root user (SECURITY.md).

  deploy: {replicas: 2}

question: Describe the scaling path of this engine at 10x and 100x load.
answer_hinglish:
Pehle current baseline: TESTING.md ke hisaab se (Postgres in Docker Desktop on Windows) ek worker process ~4.9 workflows/s, 4 processes ~8.3 workflows/s, aur ek 4-activity workflow ~97 SQL statements leta hai. Ek process CPU-bound hai (80% wall). Toh bottlenecks do hain: worker CPU (replay + Python overhead) aur shared Postgres.

10x: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ka plan -- (1) zyada worker processes, kyunki processes scale karte hain, in-process workers nahi; (2) per-type task queues taaki slow activities fast ones ko block na karein (code per-activity `task_queue` already support karta hai); (3) sticky cache -- jis worker ne workflow last chalaya woh state memory mein rakhe aur sirf naye events apply kare, full replay sirf cache miss pe. Saath mein SQL statements kam karna: batch history reads, fewer round trips, aur polling interval tune ya LISTEN/NOTIFY.

100x: ek Postgres nahi chalega. Workflows ko `workflow_id` hash se shards mein baanto -- Temporal ke "history shards" -- har shard ka apna DB/partition, aur har workflow ke saare writes ek shard pe (row lock semantics intact). Task queues ke liye alag matching service jo in-memory hai aur push-based delivery karti hai (long-poll), DB polling nahi. Timers ke liye per-shard timer queues. Aur long histories ke liye continue-as-new taaki replay cost bounded rahe.

Main honest rahunga: is project mein sticky cache, sharding, matching service, continue-as-new -- kuch bhi implement nahi hai; yeh documented path hai.
why_needed: System design rounds mein 'aaj kya hai' se 'kal kaise badhega' tak ka roadmap expected hota hai, measurements ke saath.
real_world_analogy: Ek counter wala bank: pehle aur cashiers (workers), phir alag counters per kaam (task queues), phir alag branches (shards) jahan har customer ka account ek hi branch mein.
how_it_works: Scale ke liye contention points tod do: CPU (processes, sticky cache), DB (statements kam, shards), polling (push), history length (continue-as-new).
in_this_project: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` "Scaling path" table; `TESTING.md` benchmarks; `bench/bench.py::throughput_processes`; `runtime.py::execute_activity` ka `task_queue` param; `store.py::claim_workflow_task` single DB.

disadvantages: Sharding ke saath cross-shard queries (list/stats) mehenge
Matching service = naya stateful component

question: You need a production-grade charge_payment activity against a real payment provider. What changes compared to the demo activity?
answer_hinglish:
Demo `charge_payment` sirf `card` string dekh ke fail/flaky simulate karta hai aur `activity_effects` mein row likhta hai. Real provider ke saath paanch cheezein badalti hain.

Ek, idempotency pass-through: `ctx.idempotency_key` (`workflow_id:seq`) ko provider ke Idempotency-Key header mein bhejo. Retry ya redelivery pe provider wahi charge return karega, naya nahi banayega. Yeh engine ke at-least-once model ka natural partner hai.

Do, error classification: card declined, invalid card, insufficient funds -- `NonRetryableError` raise karo (ya error type ko `RetryPolicy.non_retryable_errors` mein list karo), kyunki retry se kuch nahi badlega. Network timeout, 5xx, 429 -- normal exception, retry with backoff. Galat classification = ya toh customer ko 3 baar decline, ya transient error pe permanent fail.

Teen, timeouts: HTTP client timeout `start_to_close` se chhota rakho, warna `asyncio.wait_for` activity ko cancel karega aur aapko pata nahi chalega request gayi ya nahi. Ambiguous outcome pe retry hi sahi hai -- idempotency key bachayegi.

Chaar, retry policy: payment ke liye `maximum_attempts` sochke -- unlimited nahi; `maximum_interval` provider ke rate limits ke hisaab se.

Paanch, result: workflow ko sirf zaroori data return karo (charge_id, amount), poora provider response nahi -- woh history mein permanently jaata hai aur plaintext hai (SECURITY.md: secrets history mein mat daalo; card number kabhi nahi, token/reference hi).

question: What operational concerns arise when workflows run for weeks or months?
answer_hinglish:
`customer_onboarding` ka comment hai "durable timer: days in real life" -- yeh engine mahine-bhar chalne wale workflows ke liye hai. Lambi umar chaar problems laati hai.

Ek, code evolution: mahine mein aap kai deploys karoge, aur har running workflow ko har naye code se replay hona hai. Toh versioning discipline (naya workflow type ya `patched()`, jo is project mein implement nahi hai) aur CI replay checks mandatory hain.

Do, history growth: har signal/timer/activity event jodta hai. Agar workflow loop mein hai (har din reminder) toh history badhti hi jaayegi aur replay cost super-linear hai (TESTING.md: 2,001 events ~102-132 ms). Production fix continue-as-new hai -- yahan implement nahi hai.

Teen, far-future timers: `ctx.sleep(30 days)` sirf `timers` table mein row hai (`fire_at`), koi process memory mein wait nahi karta -- isliye restarts ka koi asar nahi. Par `fire_at` worker ki clock se compute hota hai (`datetime.now(timezone.utc)` in `complete_workflow_task`) jabki leases DB `now()` use karte hain -- clock skew ho toh timer thoda jaldi/der se. Mahino mein yeh negligible, par seconds-level timers ke liye noticeable (observation).

Chaar, data aur dependencies: activity ka external API mahine mein badal sakta hai, input schema purana ho sakta hai, aur retention -- `DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 4 bolta hai closed workflows ki history N din baad archive karo; running ones ki history toh chahiye hi.

Plus visibility: dashboard pe 'running' workflows ka list bada hota jaata hai; filter by age/type chahiye.
why_needed: Durable execution ka value hi long-running processes mein hai; unki operational costs samajhna senior-level expectation hai.
real_world_analogy: Lambi train journey: beech mein driver badalte hain (deploys), log chadhte-utarte hain (events), aur timetable alag shehron ki ghadiyon se match karna padta hai (clock skew).
how_it_works: Long wait = DB row (timer) ya pending signal waiter, koi resource nahi. Har wake-up pe full replay, isliye history size hi asli cost hai.
in_this_project: `flowengine/examples/workflows.py::customer_onboarding` (`ctx.sleep(inp["tips_after"])`), `flowengine/store.py::complete_workflow_task` (timer `fire_at` worker clock se), `flowengine/store.py::fire_due_timers`, `DEPLOYMENT.md` retention rule, README known limitations (no continue-as-new).

question: Explain Temporal's history shards and matching service in depth, and what flowengine would need to adopt them.
answer_hinglish:
Temporal server mein chaar services hain: Frontend (API gateway), History, Matching, aur internal Worker. History service workflows ko fixed number of shards mein baantti hai -- shard = hash(workflow_id) mod N, aur N cluster create karte waqt fix hota hai. Har shard ek time pe ek history host ka owner hota hai (membership ring), aur us shard ke saare workflows ki mutable state, history appends, timers aur transfer tasks wahi process karta hai. Isse ek workflow ke writes serialize hote hain bina global lock ke -- jaise humara workflow row lock, par distributed.

Shard ke andar "transfer queue" hai: jab history mein ActivityScheduled likha jaata hai, usi transaction mein ek transfer task bhi likha jaata hai (outbox jaisa) jo baad mein Matching service ko activity task push karta hai. Timer queue durable timers fire karti hai.

Matching service task queues manage karti hai, partitions mein baanti hui. Workers long-poll karte hain; task aaya toh seedha in-memory "sync match" se waiting poller ko de diya jaata hai, DB mein persist kiye bina. Poller nahi hai tab task persist hota hai (backlog).

flowengine mein: single Postgres = ek shard; `needs_task` + `activity_tasks` table = matching; `_timer_loop` = timer queue; aur hum ek hi transaction mein history + task insert karte hain, isliye transfer queue ki zaroorat nahi. Adopt karne ke liye: workflow_id hash se N databases/partitions, har shard ka owner process (lease-based), shard ke andar outbox se tasks matching tak, aur matching ek alag long-poll service. Yeh is project mein implement nahi hai -- `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` 100x row mein documented hai.
why_needed: Temporal-style project ke saath interviewer naturally poochhega 'yeh real Temporal se kaise alag hai aur scale kaise karega'.
real_world_analogy: Bade bank mein har account number ek fixed branch (shard) ka; branch ka manager (owner host) us account ka har transaction serialize karta hai. Token counter (matching) customers ko khaali cashier se jodta hai -- line mein koi wait kar raha hai toh seedha bhej do.
how_it_works: Fixed shard count + consistent ownership; per-shard transactional writes; outbox (transfer queue) for cross-service delivery; sync match for low latency; DB backlog only when no poller.
in_this_project: `flowengine/store.py::complete_workflow_task` (history + activity task + timer same tx -- humare paas transfer queue nahi), `flowengine/store.py::claim_activity` (DB polling = our matching), `flowengine/worker.py::_timer_loop`. `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` scaling path, README "Single Postgres is the bottleneck".

N_SHARDS = 16
def shard_of(workflow_id: str) -> int:
    return zlib.crc32(workflow_id.encode()) % N_SHARDS       # fixed forever: resharding = migration
sm = SHARD_SESSIONMAKERS[shard_of(wid)]
await store.signal(sm, wid, "approve", payload)

Cross-shard listing ke liye alag visibility store

History aur task dispatch ko alag transactions mein likhna bina outbox ke
Matching ko source of truth maan lena

advanced.failure_scenarios: Shard ownership split-brain -> do hosts same shard likhein; Temporal range ids (fencing tokens) se purane owner ke writes reject karta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Citus/Vitess se Postgres shard karna, Cassandra (Temporal default), FoundationDB, ya Kafka partitions as shards.

question: Child workflows, queries and schedules are missing. What are they and how would you add each to this engine?
answer_hinglish:
README ke known limitations mein likha hai: "no child workflows, queries, or schedules (cron)". Teeno ka matlab aur design:

Child workflow: ek workflow doosra workflow start kare aur uska result await kare -- jaise `order_processing` har item ke liye ek `fulfil_item` child. Add karne ke liye naya command `start_child` (seq ke saath), complete_workflow_task mein `ChildWorkflowStarted` event + `store.start_workflow` (child id deterministic, e.g. `parent:seq`, taaki idempotent start reuse ho), aur jab child close ho toh parent ki history mein `ChildWorkflowCompleted/Failed` append + parent ka `needs_task = true`. Parent cancel pe child ko bhi cancel (parent close policy).

Query: running workflow ka state padhna bina history badle -- "abhi kitne emails gaye?". Implementation: history load karo, replay karo (jaise `replay-check` endpoint karta hai), aur `ctx` pe registered query handler ko call karo; kuch append nahi. Key rule: query handler read-only aur deterministic.

Schedule (cron): har din 9 baje naya run. Ek `schedules` table (cron expr, next_fire_at, workflow_type, input) aur timer loop jaisa poller jo `start_workflow(workflow_id = f"{sched}:{fire_time}")` call kare -- deterministic id se duplicate fire bhi idempotent ho jaata hai.

Teeno existing pieces reuse karte hain: idempotent start, history events, needs_task, replay. Is project mein yeh implement nahi hai; yeh design hai.
why_needed: Real workflows composable hote hain aur operators ko running state dekhni hoti hai; interviewer feature gaps ke design dekhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Child = manager ka kaam team member ko dena aur report ka wait; query = manager ka 'status kya hai?' poochhna bina kaam badle; schedule = har subah alarm.
how_it_works: Har feature ek naya command/event type ya ek naya poller hai; durability history se aur idempotency deterministic ids se aati hai.
in_this_project: README "Known limitations"; reuse points: `flowengine/store.py::start_workflow` (idempotent on workflow_id), `flowengine/api.py::replay_check` (read-only replay -- query ka base), `flowengine/worker.py::_timer_loop` (schedules ke liye pattern).

# illustrative: query via read-only replay (NOT in repo)
@router.get("/workflows/{workflow_id}/query/{name}")
async def query(workflow_id: str, name: str, request: Request):
    wf = await store.describe(request.app.state.sm, workflow_id)
    events = await store.history(request.app.state.sm, workflow_id)
    ctx_holder = {}
    await replay(WORKFLOWS[wf["workflow_type"]], workflow_id, str(wf["run_id"]), events, on_ctx=ctx_holder.setdefault)
    return {"result": ctx_holder["ctx"].queries[name]()}   # needs replay() to expose ctx + ctx.queries registry

Query har baar full replay (sticky cache ke bina mehenga)

question: End to end, what is exactly-once in this engine and what is only at-least-once?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh precise bolna padta hai, kyunki "exactly-once" loosely bolna interview mein red flag hai.

Exactly-once (engine level, DB transactions se): (1) history append -- har event gap-free id ke saath ek hi baar, kyunki `_append` workflow row lock ke andar hai aur PK `(workflow_id, event_id)` hai. (2) Command scheduling -- `activity_tasks UNIQUE(workflow_id, seq)` aur optimistic commit (`last_event_id` check) ensure karte hain ki ek command do baar schedule na ho, chahe do workers same workflow replay karein. (3) Activity result recording -- `complete_activity` fenced update (`status = 'started' AND attempt = :a`) ke baad hi `ActivityCompleted` append karta hai, toh ek attempt ka result hi history mein jaata hai. (4) Timer firing -- `UPDATE timers SET fired = true ... AND NOT fired`. (5) Workflow start -- workflow_id PK.

At-least-once: activity execution. Worker crash, lease expiry, ya complete commit fail -- activity dobara chalegi. Workflow code ka execution bhi many-times hai (har replay), par woh pure hai toh koi asar nahi.

Effectively-once (application ki zimmedari): side effects. `idempotency_key = workflow_id:seq` + downstream dedupe (`activity_effects` ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING). Tests exact effect counts assert karte hain, jaise 20 workflows on 2 workers pe `{"reserve": 20, "charge": 20, "ship": 20, "email": 20}`.

Review mein mila gap (ab fixed): pehle workflow close hone ke baad bhi running activity ka completion history mein append ho jaata tha, aur cancel sirf 'scheduled' tasks cancel karta tha -- closed workflow ki started activity reap hoke retry ho sakti thi. Fix: cancel/close 'started' bhi cancel karte hain aur `complete_activity`/`fail_activity` mein `_closed()` guard -- post-close kuch append nahi hota (tests `test_cancel_stops_running_activity_and_it_is_never_retried`, `test_late_activity_completion_after_close_appends_nothing`). Activity execution phir bhi at-least-once hi hai.
why_needed: Distributed systems interviews mein delivery semantics ka precise vocabulary sabse zyada test hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Post office: registry book mein entry exactly once (DB), postman ek letter do baar la sakta hai (at-least-once), aap envelope number dekh ke dusri copy phenk dete ho (effectively-once).
how_it_works: DB transactions + unique constraints + fencing internal state ko exactly-once banate hain; external world ke saath sirf at-least-once + idempotency possible hai.
in_this_project: `flowengine/store.py::_append`, `complete_workflow_task`, `complete_activity` (fenced), `fire_due_timers` (`AND NOT fired`), `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` (UNIQUE (workflow_id, seq)). Test: `tests/test_engine.py::test_two_workers_process_many_workflows_without_duplicates`.

# real, flowengine/store.py (complete_activity): fenced, so only the owning attempt records a result
res = await s.execute(text("UPDATE activity_tasks SET status = 'completed', lease_until = NULL WHERE id = :i "
                           "AND status = 'started' AND attempt = :a"), {"i": task["id"], "a": task["attempt"]})
if res.rowcount == 0:
    return False          # fenced: our lease expired and another attempt owns it

Non-heartbeating activity cancel ke baad bhi apna external effect kar sakti hai

Workflow code mein side effect karna kyunki 'woh ek baar chalta hai'
Fencing ke bina completion likhna

question: How could long activities resume from their last heartbeat checkpoint instead of restarting? Is that implemented?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein yeh implement nahi hai. Abhi heartbeat do kaam karta hai: lease extend karna aur progress `heartbeat_details` column mein store karna. `long_task` har chunk ke baad `ctx.heartbeat({"done": i + 1})` bhejta hai, aur heartbeat test `heartbeat_details->>'done'` padh ke dekhta hai ki 3 chunks ho gaye. Par jab worker A crash hota hai aur worker B attempt 2 claim karta hai, toh `ActivityContext` mein previous details ka koi field hi nahi hai -- B chunk 0 se dobara shuru karta hai. 10 chunks ke liye theek hai, par 3 ghante ka data export ho toh poora kaam waste.

Temporal mein yeh feature hai: `activity.info().heartbeat_details` next attempt ko last recorded details deta hai, aur activity wahan se continue karti hai.

Add karna simple hai: (1) `ActivityContext` mein `heartbeat_details: Any = None` field; (2) `Worker._execute` mein `task["heartbeat_details"]` pass karo -- `claim_activity` `RETURNING *` already column return karta hai; (3) `claim_activity` heartbeat_details ko reset nahi karta, toh value attempts ke across survive karti hai -- good; (4) activity code `start = (ctx.heartbeat_details or {}).get("done", 0)` se loop shuru kare.

Important caveat: checkpoint "jitna kaam hua" ka hint hai, guarantee nahi. Crash heartbeat ke baad aur agle chunk ke beech hua ho toh last chunk ka kaam ho chuka par details purani -- isliye chunk-level kaam bhi idempotent hona chahiye (e.g. chunk key `idempotency_key:chunk_i`).
why_needed: Lambi activities (batch processing, exports) mein restart ka cost bahut bada hota hai; checkpointing practical necessity hai.
real_world_analogy: Video game ka checkpoint: game crash hua toh shuru se nahi, last save point se. Par last save ke baad jo kiya woh dobara karna padega.
how_it_works: Heartbeat -> DB mein details. Next claim -> row mein details already hain -> context mein pass -> activity skip karti hai completed chunks.
in_this_project: `flowengine/examples/activities.py::long_task` heartbeat bhejta hai; `flowengine/store.py::heartbeat` details store karta hai; `flowengine/activities.py::ActivityContext` mein details field nahi hai; `tests/test_engine.py::test_activity_heartbeat_timeout_detects_dead_worker` progress padhta hai.

question: Temporal SDKs use a custom deterministic event loop. How does flowengine get determinism from standard asyncio instead, and where can that break?
answer_hinglish:
Temporal Python SDK workflow code ko ek custom asyncio event loop pe chalata hai (sandbox ke saath) -- woh loop sirf workflow ke futures schedule karta hai, real time nahi deta, aur threads/IO ko block karta hai. Har activation pe woh "run until no more progress" karta hai.

flowengine standard asyncio loop pe hi chalta hai aur ek chhota trick use karta hai: `_settle()`. Workflow coroutine ek Task hai; settle `asyncio.sleep(0)` teen baar karta hai (taaki pending callbacks chal jaayein) aur phir state tuple compare karta hai -- `(task.done(), len(ctx.commands), done futures count)`. State na badle toh maana jaata hai coroutine sirf unresolved ctx futures pe ruka hai. Determinism isliye aata hai ki futures sirf replay loop resolve karta hai, events ke recorded order mein, aur har resolve ke baad settle.

Kahan toot sakta hai: (1) Agar workflow code real `asyncio.sleep(1)` ya network await kare toh settle usse "ruka hua" samjhega, replay aage badh jaayega -- result non-deterministic. Custom loop yeh block karta, humara nahi; sirf convention (`SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` rules) hai. (2) Agar ek await chain mein teen se zyada hops lage aur state tuple same dikhe toh settle jaldi return ho sakta hai -- loop tab tak chalta hai jab tak state badle, isliye practical mein theek hai, par yeh heuristic hai, proof nahi. (3) Wall clock, `random`, global state access -- koi sandbox nahi rokta.

Benefit: code chhota (~250 lines runtime) aur normal asyncio primitives (`gather`, `wait`) kaam karte hain -- `email_campaign` gather use karta hai.
why_needed: Determinism engine ki foundation hai; interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki aap mechanism aur uski limits dono jaante ho.
real_world_analogy: Exam hall mein invigilator (custom loop) phone use karne hi nahi deta; humare yahan sirf rule board laga hai 'phone mana hai' -- honest student ke saath kaam karta hai.
how_it_works: Single coroutine Task + futures controlled by replay + settle heuristic = deterministic progression, provided code awaits only ctx futures.
in_this_project: `flowengine/runtime.py::_settle` aur `flowengine/runtime.py::replay`; docstring "A workflow is ordinary async Python that may only await things it gets from the WorkflowContext". `tests/test_runtime.py::test_parallel_activities_with_gather` dikhata hai gather kaam karta hai. Sandbox/linting is project mein implement nahi hai.

Settle heuristic hai
common_mistakes: Workflow mein asyncio.sleep use karna ctx.sleep ki jagah
datetime.now() workflow mein
Workflow code mein DB/HTTP call

question: Orchestration vs choreography for sagas: when would you choose an event-driven Kafka choreography over this orchestrated engine?
answer_hinglish:
Orchestration (yeh project): ek central workflow (`order_processing`) decide karta hai kaun sa step kab, aur failure pe kaun si compensation -- poora flow ek file mein readable hai. Choreography: koi central controller nahi; services events publish karti hain (`OrderPlaced`, `PaymentCharged`, `ShipmentFailed`) aur doosri services react karti hain -- Kafka (Project 5 jaisa log) iska typical backbone hai.

Orchestration ke fayde: flow ek jagah, compensation logic explicit try/except mein, history/dashboard pe ek workflow ka poora timeline, timeouts aur waiting (signals, timers) native. `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` bolta hai durable orchestration ki wajah se compensations crash ke baad bhi guaranteed chalti hain -- hand-written sagas ki sabse badi kamzori.

Choreography ke fayde: services loosely coupled, koi central dependency nahi, naya consumer bina orchestrator change kiye add ho sakta hai, aur throughput high (Kafka partitions). Jahan facts broadcast karne hain aur consumers independent hain (analytics, notifications, search indexing) -- choreography. Practical systems dono mix karte hain: orchestrated workflow ek activity se event publish kare.

question: Write a pure replay test proving that replacing a durable timer with an activity is detected as non-determinism. What happens in the reverse case?
answer_hinglish:
Task: `tests/test_runtime.py` mein hand-built history ke saath ek test likhna. Yeh tests DB ke bina chalte hain, isliye fast hain aur exactly replay logic ko target karte hain.

Setup: purane code ne `ctx.sleep(60)` kiya tha, toh history mein `WorkflowStarted` aur `TimerStarted(seq=1)` hai. Naya code seq 1 pe `execute_activity("send_reminder")` produce karta hai. `replay()` jab `TimerStarted` event dekhta hai, woh `ctx.commands[1]` nikalta hai aur check karta hai `cmd.kind != "start_timer"` -- yahan kind `schedule_activity` hai, toh `NonDeterminismError`. Test `pytest.raises` se yeh assert karta hai.

Reverse case interesting hai -- aur yeh ek real bug tha jo interview bank likhte waqt code review mein mila: history mein `ActivityScheduled(seq=1, activity_type="reserve")` aur naya code seq 1 pe `ctx.sleep(5)`. Replay code pehle `cmd.attrs["activity_type"]` padhta tha -- par timer command ke attrs mein sirf `seconds` hai, toh `NonDeterminismError` nahi, `KeyError` aata tha. Worker ka `run_workflow_task_once` sirf `NonDeterminismError` pakadta hai, toh KeyError `_workflow_loop` ke generic `except Exception` mein log hota, `error` column set nahi hota, aur lease expire hoke task baar-baar retry hota -- operator ko dashboard pe kuch nahi dikhta.

Fix ek line tha: `cmd.attrs.get("activity_type")`. Regression test ab repo mein hai: `tests/test_review_fixes.py::test_timer_where_history_has_activity_is_nondeterminism_not_keyerror` (`pytest.raises(NonDeterminismError)`, jo KeyError pe fail hota). Story: bug -> root cause -> one-line fix -> test jo purane code pe fail hota hai.
why_needed: Determinism detection engine ka safety net hai; uske har branch ke tests chahiye, warna bad deploy galat tarike se fail hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Fire alarm test: sirf dhuan wala sensor test kiya, garmi wala nahi -- aag lagi toh pata chala alarm bajta hi nahi.

question: Implement a Temporal-style ctx.patched(change_id) so new runs take a new code path while running workflows keep the old one.
answer_hinglish:
Requirement: `order_processing` mein charge se pehle `fraud_check` add karna hai, par jo orders already chal rahe hain unki history mein woh step nahi -- unhe purana path lena hai, warna NonDeterminismError.

Temporal semantics: `patched(id)` -- (1) agar history mein `MarkerRecorded(id)` hai toh True; (2) agar hum abhi history replay kar rahe hain (aur marker nahi mila) toh False -- yeh purana run hai; (3) agar replay khatam ho chuka (naya code path pe naye commands ban rahe hain) toh marker record karo aur True.

Implementation choices: marker ko `seq` nahi dena, warna baad ke saare seq numbers shift ho jaate aur purane runs ka matching toot jaata. Isliye markers alag list mein, `Command(0, "marker", ...)` ke roop mein `new_commands` ke aage. `replay()` mein history pre-scan karke markers ka set banta hai, aur `_replaying` flag tab tak True rehta hai jab tak aakhri event feed na ho. `MarkerRecorded` event replay loop mein bas skip hota hai. `complete_workflow_task` mein `marker` kind ka event append hota hai -- koi task/timer nahi.

Edge: purana run jo `patched()` tak tab pahunche jab saari history feed ho chuki (jaise aakhri event signal tha) -- woh naya path lega. Yeh sahi hai kyunki uske aage ke commands abhi history mein hain hi nahi. Cleanup: jab saare purane runs close ho jaayein, `patched` hata ke sirf naya path rakho (Temporal ka `deprecate_patch` step). Is project mein yeh feature abhi implement nahi hai -- README isko gap bolta hai.

question: How does the retry-task admin operation resume a workflow blocked by a NonDeterminismError after the fix is deployed, and why was it added?
answer_hinglish:
Problem: `complete_workflow_task` non-determinism pe `error` set karta hai aur `needs_task = false` kar deta hai. Fixed code deploy hone ke baad koi bhi cheez workflow ko dobara pick nahi karti jab tak naya event (signal/timer/activity completion) na aaye. Code review mein mila ki iske liye koi API thi hi nahi -- `test_nondeterministic_deploy_is_detected_and_workflow_survives` khud raw SQL `UPDATE workflows SET needs_task = true` chalata tha. Operational gap.

Fix do layer mein (ab repo mein): `store.retry_workflow_task(sm, workflow_id)` -- workflow row lock, status `running` nahi toh `Conflict` ('workflow is cancelled' etc.), warna `needs_task = true`, aur return `{workflow_id, requeued: True, previous_error}`. `error` clear nahi hota; agla successful `complete_workflow_task` khud `error = NULL` karta hai, aur fix kaam na kare toh naya error overwrite hota hai -- operator ko evidence milta rehta hai. API: `POST /workflows/{id}/retry-task` (`api.py::retry_task`), header `X-Admin-Token` ko `settings.admin_token` se compare karta hai -- pehle yeh config field kahin use nahi hoti thi. Docstring: pehle `replay-check` chalao.

Tests: `test_retry_task_requeues_only_running_workflows` (blocked -> requeued + previous_error; cancelled workflow pe exception) aur non-determinism test ab raw UPDATE ki jagah `store.retry_workflow_task` use karta hai.

Token check `hmac.compare_digest` se hota hai (constant-time; pehle `!=` tha, jo timing se batata hai ki kitne leading characters match hue -- review mein pakda aur fix kiya). Aage ke improvements: bulk version (`WHERE error LIKE 'NonDeterminismError%'`) deploy pipeline ke last step ke liye.

real_world_analogy: Machine jam hui toh mechanic theek karta hai, phir 'restart' button dabata hai -- seedha wiring nahi chhedta.

question: Make the determinism check optionally compare activity arguments, so inserting a same-type step (bug 5) is detected.
answer_hinglish:
Background: `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` bug 5 -- type-level check same activity type ka inserted step nahi pakadta. Accha news: `complete_workflow_task` `ActivityScheduled` event mein `args` already store karta hai (`{"seq", "activity_type", "args", "retry"}`). Toh compare karne ke liye data history mein hai, sirf check missing hai.

Design: `replay(..., strict_args=False)` keyword. Default off rakha kyunki Temporal-compatible behaviour hai aur argument-level bug fixes (template name change) running workflows ko block nahi karne chahiye. Strict mode CI ke replay-check mein ya specific workflow types ke liye on karo.

Normalisation zaroori hai: history se args JSONB round-trip ke baad aate hain (tuples lists ban jaate hain, datetime string ban jaata hai via `_j` ka `default=str`). Isliye dono sides `json.loads(json.dumps(x, default=str))` se normalise -- exactly wahi transformation jo store karte waqt hua. Hand-built test histories mein `args` nahi hota, isliye check sirf tab jab `"args" in a`.

KeyError gap (timer command mein activity_type nahi hota) review mein pehle hi fix ho chuka hai -- `cmd.attrs.get("activity_type")` aur test `test_timer_where_history_has_activity_is_nondeterminism_not_keyerror` -- isliye strict mode bhi `.get` hi use karta hai.

Test: v1 `notify("x", "step 1")`; v2 pehle `notify("x", "audit")` insert karta hai. Default mode mein replay pass (bug 5 reproduce), strict mode mein `NonDeterminismError`. Yeh dono asserts ek test mein -- documentation ki tarah kaam karte hain.
why_needed: Same-type insert silently galat results deta hai (purane step ka result naye step ko) -- sabse dangerous non-determinism kyunki error hi nahi aata.
real_world_analogy: Sirf parcel ka size check karna vs size + address dono check karna -- same size ka galat parcel ab pakda jaayega.

question: When wait_signal's signal wins, the timeout timer still fires later. Implement timer cancellation without breaking running workflows.
answer_hinglish:
Observation: `wait_signal(name, timeout)` andar `self.sleep(timeout)` se timer banata hai. Signal jeet gaya toh woh future ko ignore karta hai, par `timers` table ki row abhi bhi `fired = false` hai. Baad mein `fire_due_timers` `TimerFired` append karta hai aur `needs_task = true` -- ek bekaar workflow task (full replay) aur history mein extra event. `_resolve` mein `if fut.done(): return` hai, isliye correctness break nahi hoti, sirf waste. `document_approval` ka escalate_after 3600 jaisa timeout ho toh ek ghante baad yeh ghost wake-up aayega.

Fix design: naya command `cancel_timer` -> event `TimerCanceled(seq)` + timer row `fired = true`. Sabse important constraint: yeh command `seq` consume NAHI kar sakta. Agar kare toh signal-jeete purane runs mein agla activity seq ek aage shift ho jaayega aur replay NonDeterminismError dega. Isliye cancel commands alag list mein (`Command(0, ...)`), jaise patched ke markers.

Determinism: code tabhi cancel command produce kare jab history mein us seq ka `TimerFired` ya `TimerCanceled` already na ho -- isliye replay start pe history se `_closed_timers` set banta hai. Race: timer fire ho raha tha jab hum replay kar rahe the -> `last_event_id` badla -> optimistic commit reject -> agla replay `TimerFired` dekhega aur cancel produce nahi karega. Store side mein `UPDATE timers SET fired = true ... AND NOT fired` workflow row lock ke andar chalta hai, aur `fire_due_timers` bhi pehle workflow row lock karta hai, toh dono serialize hote hain.

Test: pure replay -- signal pehle aaya toh new_commands mein `cancel_timer` hai; history mein `TimerCanceled` hai toh dobara nahi.
why_needed: Ghost wake-ups CPU (full replay) aur history size dono waste karte hain; scale pe yeh significant hai.
real_world_analogy: Alarm laga ke so gaye, phir khud hi jaldi uth gaye -- alarm band karna bhool gaye toh ghante baad bajega aur ghar wale uth jaayenge.
how_it_works: Signal win -> cancel command (no seq) -> commit: TimerCanceled event + timer row fired=true -> fire_due_timers usse kabhi pick nahi karta.
in_this_project: `flowengine/runtime.py::wait_signal` (timer ignore hota hai), `flowengine/runtime.py::_resolve` (done future pe return), `flowengine/store.py::fire_due_timers`, `flowengine/store.py::complete_workflow_task`. Test pattern: `tests/test_runtime.py::test_race_signal_first_wins`.

disadvantages: Naya event type aur store branch
Purane runs ke already-pending timers phir bhi fire honge (theek hai)
common_mistakes: Cancel command ko seq dena
Timer row DELETE karna bina event (history aur DB out of sync)
History check ke bina har replay pe cancel produce karna
follow_up_questions: Workflow close hone pe saare pending timers cancel kyun nahi?
Temporal mein timer cancel kaise hota hai?
Kitna replay CPU bachega estimate kaise karoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Extra event type complexity vs bekaar replays; seq-free commands compatibility dete hain par seq ke 'har command ek number' invariant ko todte hain.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Cancel aur fire ka race -- workflow row lock + optimistic commit se serialize; agar commit reject hua toh agla replay sahi decision leta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Workflow close pe saare unfired timers mark karna (simpler, partial fix); timer row pe 'owner future' check jo fire karne se pehle workflow state dekhe.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x pe har signal-with-timeout workflow ek extra replay deta -- cancellation se workflow tasks noticeably kam.
advanced.production_improvements: Metric: TimerFired events whose future was already done (ghost fires), alert agar high; workflow close pe timer cleanup.
